solution: Take out the common factor of each pair, ${=c}$ from the first pair and $j$ from the second pair: $({=c*p}m + {=c*q}n) + ({=p}jm + {=q}jn) = {=c}({=p}m + {=q}n) + j({=p}m + {=q}n)$.
Both terms now contain the same binomial $({=p}m + {=q}n)$, so take it out as a common factor: ${=c}({=p}m + {=q}n) + j({=p}m + {=q}n) = ({=p}m + {=q}n)({=c} + j)$.
Check by expanding: $({=p}m + {=q}n)({=c} + j) = {=c*p}m + {=p}jm + {=c*q}n + {=q}jn$, which has the same four terms as the original expression.
notes: Basic tier: the entry point of grouping in pairs. It is the exact skeleton of book question ex1-11-30e (14m-4n+7jm-2jn = 2(7m-2n)+j(7m-2n) = (7m-2n)(2+j)) with every sign positive, so the learner meets the pair-and-common-binomial idea before having to handle subtraction signs (the standard book exercises). The expression is built as c*p*m + c*q*n + p*j*m + q*j*n, so the terms already sit in the order that the pairs are the first two and the last two; the first pair's common factor is the number c, the second pair's is the letter j, and the two brackets are identical (p*m + q*n), exactly as in the book solution. Parameter choices: p, q in 2..7 and c in 2..6, so every coefficient is a plain whole number of at most 42 and no coefficient of 1 (which would need the letter printed bare) ever occurs. gcd(p, q) = 1 guarantees the binomial (p*m + q*n) has no further common factor, so the answer is fully factorised and the first pair's greatest common factor is exactly c; p and q are therefore never equal. c >= 2 guarantees the first pair needs a visible numerical common factor (never a factor of 1). Alternative grouping (first with third term, second with fourth) gives the same factorised answer (p*m + q*n)(c + j) up to the order of factors, so the marker is unambiguous. No distractors (not an mcq), hence no misconception ids; none are catalogued for this objective. The variable j is used as an ordinary letter, as in the book question; if the marker's parser treats j as the imaginary unit, rename j to another letter (for example k) in the stem, solution and marker together.
